title: Cybersecurity Analyst
subtitle: Climb the money ladder -- one analyst question per grade level

gradeLabels.f: F-RANK -- Back to the Alert Queue

questions.q: What is the primary function of a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system?
options: Encrypt hard drives and enforce full-disk security policies
Block inbound and outbound traffic like a next-generation firewall
Collect and correlate logs from many sources to detect and alert on security events
Scan endpoints for malware signatures like an antivirus engine
questions.note: A SIEM aggregates log data across the environment and correlates events to surface alerts -- it does not block traffic or scan for malware itself.

explain.correct: A SIEM collects logs and telemetry from many sources (firewalls, endpoints, servers), correlates them against rules and baselines, and raises alerts when suspicious patterns emerge.
wrong: Disk encryption is performed by tools like BitLocker or VeraCrypt, not a SIEM.
Firewalls block traffic; a SIEM is a passive detection and alerting platform, not an enforcement point.
Antivirus engines scan for malware signatures on the endpoint; a SIEM analyzes log data, not files.

questions.q: Which framework is specifically designed to catalog adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) observed in real-world intrusions?
options: OWASP Top 10
PCI DSS
ISO 9001
MITRE ATT&CK
questions.note: MITRE ATT&CK is the industry-standard TTP knowledge base; the other options are a web-risk list, a payment standard, and a quality-management standard respectively.

explain.correct: MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) documents the tactics (goals) and techniques (methods) threat actors use, mapped from real incident data.
wrong: OWASP Top 10 ranks the ten most critical web-application security risks -- it is not a TTP framework covering all adversary behavior.
PCI DSS is a compliance standard for organizations that handle cardholder data, not a threat-intel framework.
ISO 9001 is a quality-management system standard with no direct cybersecurity scope.

questions.q: A SOC analyst sees Windows Security Event ID 4625 firing repeatedly for the same account. What activity does this event record?
options: A new process was created on the system
An account was successfully locked out after threshold exceeded
A user successfully logged on to the system
A user failed to log on to the system
questions.note: Event ID 4625 = failed logon; 4624 = successful logon; 4688 = new process creation. Repeated 4625s are a classic brute-force or password-spray indicator.

explain.correct: Windows Security Event ID 4625 is generated every time an account fails to authenticate. Multiple 4625 events for one account in a short window are a primary brute-force indicator.
wrong: New process creation is logged under Event ID 4688, not 4625.
Account lockout generates Event ID 4740; 4625 is the individual failed-logon event that precedes a lockout.
Successful logon is Event ID 4624 -- the most common confusion pairing with 4625.

questions.q: A vulnerability scanner reports a CVSS v3.1 base score of 7.5 for a finding. Which severity band does this score fall into?
options: Medium (4.0-6.9)
Critical (9.0-10.0)
questions.note: CVSS v3.1 bands: None=0.0, Low=0.1-3.9, Medium=4.0-6.9, High=7.0-8.9, Critical=9.0-10.0. A score of 7.5 sits squarely in High.

explain.correct: Under CVSS v3.1, scores from 7.0 through 8.9 are classified as High severity. A score of 7.5 is above the Medium ceiling (6.9) and below the Critical floor (9.0).
wrong: Medium covers 4.0-6.9. A score of 7.5 exceeds the Medium ceiling of 6.9.
Critical requires a score of 9.0 or above. 7.5 does not reach that threshold.
Low covers 0.1-3.9. A score of 7.5 is far above the Low ceiling.

questions.q: According to the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain, what is the FIRST stage an adversary completes before any attack can progress?
options: Reconnaissance
Weaponization
Delivery
Exploitation
questions.note: The Kill Chain order is: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives. Reconnaissance is always stage one.

explain.correct: Reconnaissance is the first stage -- the adversary gathers information about the target (open-source research, scanning, social engineering) before building any weapon or launching an attack.
wrong: Weaponization (stage 2) comes after reconnaissance -- the attacker pairs a payload with an exploit only after identifying a viable target and vector.
Delivery (stage 3) is when the weapon is transmitted to the target; it cannot happen before reconnaissance and weaponization.
Exploitation (stage 4) is when the delivered payload triggers the vulnerability -- three stages after reconnaissance.

questions.q: When preserving digital evidence, an analyst must follow the order of volatility. Among the choices below, which source must be collected FIRST because it is the most volatile?
options: The system hard disk or SSD
Backup tapes stored in the server room
RAM (system memory)
Printed log sheets kept in the operations binder
questions.note: Order of volatility (most volatile first): CPU registers/cache, RAM, network state/processes, disk, archival/print. RAM disappears on power loss and must be captured before disk or any offline media.

explain.correct: RAM is highly volatile -- its contents are lost the moment power is removed. Forensic best practice (and RFC 3227) requires capturing memory before any other source listed here, since it contains running processes, encryption keys, and network connections that no longer exist after shutdown.
wrong: Hard disk contents persist after power-off and are therefore less volatile than RAM; disk is collected after memory.
Backup tapes are non-volatile archival media -- they are the last priority in the order of volatility.
Printed logs are static records and are the least volatile source; they can be collected at any time without risk of loss.

questions.q: A threat-intel team shares indicators of compromise using STIX and TAXII. Which statement correctly describes the roles of these two standards?
options: STIX is the transport protocol; TAXII is the structured data format
Both STIX and TAXII are data formats -- one for indicators, one for reports
STIX is the structured data format for threat intelligence; TAXII is the transport protocol used to share it
Both STIX and TAXII are transport protocols for different network tiers
questions.note: STIX (Structured Threat Information eXpression) defines HOW threat data is represented; TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information) defines HOW it is transmitted between systems.

explain.correct: STIX is the standardized language (data format/schema) that describes threat objects -- indicators, campaigns, malware, threat actors. TAXII is the application-layer protocol that transports STIX bundles between sharing parties. They are complementary but serve distinct roles.
wrong: This reverses the roles. STIX is the format; TAXII is the transport -- not the other way around.
TAXII is not a data format. It is a transport protocol; STIX handles the data representation.
Neither STIX nor TAXII is a transport protocol for network tiers. STIX is a data format; only TAXII is a transport protocol.

questions.q: What are the four phases of the NIST SP 800-61 Incident Response lifecycle, listed in the correct order?
options: Preparation; Identification; Containment and Eradication; Lessons Learned
Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
Identification; Containment; Eradication; Recovery
Detection; Response; Mitigation; Reporting
questions.note: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2 defines exactly these four phases. Options A, C, and D borrow SANS PICERL or generic terminology that does not match the NIST document.

explain.correct: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2 defines the IR lifecycle as: (1) Preparation, (2) Detection and Analysis, (3) Containment, Eradication, and Recovery, and (4) Post-Incident Activity. These exact names appear in the standard.
wrong: This mixes NIST phase names with SANS PICERL language (Identification, Lessons Learned). NIST does not use Identification or Lessons Learned as phase names.
These are the SANS PICERL phases (Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery) -- a different model that is NOT NIST SP 800-61.
Detection, Response, Mitigation, and Reporting are generic IR terms, not the NIST SP 800-61 phase names.

questions.q: How does a credentialed vulnerability scan differ from an uncredentialed (unauthenticated) scan?
options: A credentialed scan only tests external-facing hosts and skips internal systems
A credentialed scan is faster but reports fewer details than an uncredentialed scan
A credentialed scan requires no authentication and relies entirely on banner grabbing
A credentialed scan logs in with valid credentials, exposing far more vulnerabilities and producing fewer false positives than an uncredentialed scan
questions.note: Credentialed scans authenticate to the target OS or application and can read patch levels, installed software, and configuration -- dramatically reducing false positives and surfacing local-privilege flaws an unauthenticated probe cannot reach.

explain.correct: By logging in with valid credentials the scanner can query the OS directly -- reading registry keys, package managers, and config files. This reveals vulnerabilities that are invisible from the network surface (e.g., missing patches on internal services) and eliminates many false positives caused by blocked or filtered probes.
wrong: The internal-vs-external distinction is unrelated to credential use. A credentialed scan can target any reachable host; scope is a separate configuration choice.
Credentialed scans are generally slower (more checks, deeper access) and report significantly MORE detail and findings, not fewer.
Banner grabbing without authentication describes an uncredentialed scan. A credentialed scan does the opposite -- it authenticates before querying.

questions.q: Malware is observed generating thousands of pseudo-random domain names each day and attempting connections to each one. Which evasion technique does this describe?
options: Fast flux -- rapidly rotating the IP addresses behind a single C2 domain
DNS over HTTPS (DoH) -- tunneling C2 traffic inside encrypted DNS queries
A Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) -- producing many pseudo-random domains so no static block list can stop C2 communications
A reverse proxy -- forwarding C2 traffic through a chain of compromised hosts
questions.note: A DGA programmatically generates large numbers of domain names; only the attacker knows which one is registered on any given day. Fast flux rotates IPs behind a domain -- a related but distinct technique.

explain.correct: A Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) is baked into the malware and produces a deterministic but pseudo-random list of domain names (often hundreds per day). Only the C2 operator registers one or a few of them. Defenders cannot block them all in advance, making static block lists ineffective.
wrong: Fast flux is a related DNS evasion technique, but it works differently: it rapidly changes the IP addresses (A records) behind a SINGLE domain name. Fast flux does not generate many domain names.
DNS over HTTPS hides DNS query content from network inspection by encrypting it, but it does not generate pseudo-random domain names.
A reverse proxy hides the true C2 server address by routing traffic through intermediaries -- it does not involve generating large numbers of pseudo-random domains.

questions.q: After compromising one workstation, an attacker uses stolen credential hashes to authenticate to a file server and then a domain controller. Which MITRE ATT&CK tactic does this describe, and how does it differ from privilege escalation?
options: Privilege Escalation -- gaining SYSTEM-level rights on the original workstation, which inherently grants access to other machines on the same subnet
Lateral Movement -- pivoting between hosts to expand network access, which is distinct from privilege escalation (gaining higher rights on the same host)
Defense Evasion -- using stolen credentials to avoid triggering alerts, which is the same concept as privilege escalation in the MITRE model
Credential Access -- harvesting password hashes from the workstation, which MITRE classifies as lateral movement when the hashes are reused
questions.note: Lateral Movement (TA0008) = using any means to move from one host to another. Privilege Escalation (TA0004) = gaining elevated rights on the CURRENT host. They are separate MITRE ATT&CK tactics with separate technique trees.

explain.correct: Lateral Movement (MITRE ATT&CK tactic TA0008) describes techniques -- such as Pass-the-Hash, Pass-the-Ticket, and RDP hijacking -- used to move from one compromised host to OTHER hosts within the network. Privilege Escalation (TA0004) is a distinct tactic covering techniques that gain higher-level permissions on the host already controlled. An analyst must distinguish them: lateral movement expands breadth (more hosts); privilege escalation expands depth (more rights on a single host).
wrong: Privilege escalation means gaining higher rights (e.g., local user to SYSTEM) on a single host. It does not describe moving between hosts, and elevated rights on one machine do not automatically grant authenticated access to other machines.

Defense Evasion (TA0005) covers techniques that help attackers avoid detection -- it is not the same as privilege escalation, and using stolen credentials to move between hosts is Lateral Movement, not Defense Evasion.

Credential Access (TA0006) covers harvesting credentials from a host. Once those credentials are used to authenticate to a different host, the action shifts to Lateral Movement. MITRE does not classify credential reuse for host-hopping as Credential Access.
